utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, could you call the case, please?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, this is case number IT-99-36-T, the Prosecutor versus Radoslav Brdjanin.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Brdjanin, can you hear me in a language that you can understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon. Yes, I can.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please be seated. Appearances for the Prosecution?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. Anna Richterova assisted by Denise Gustin, case manager.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Appearances for the Defence?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours, I'm John Ackerman, I'm here with Milan Trbojevic and Barbara Baruch. Marela Jevtovic is taking care of an administrative matter and will be here momentarily. I have handed you courtesy copies of a motion that is in the process of being filed. I think right now. To sort of provide the basis for our gathering at 5.00, and it provides basically the results of a couple of days of consideration and a meeting that we had this morning.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. I thank you. Yes. Anything else before we bring in the witness? Let's bring the witness in, please. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Good afternoon to you, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Can I ask you to stand up and repeat your solemn declaration again, please?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you. Please be seated. And Madam Richterova, you may proceed with your examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Mr. Odobasic. Yesterday we discussed this group called Wolves of Vucjak and the activities around the elections. Now I would like to discuss their activities during the year 1991 and 1992. I would like to show the witness Exhibit P82, and I have a copy for the witness. And I am referring to the attachment to the letter dated 23rd of September, 1991, which was signed by the chief of centre, security service centre, Stojan Zupljanin so I will deal with the report itself which is dated 20th September, 1991, the title is "Report on the Activity of Armed Groups on the Centre's Territory." It says, "In recent months, particularly since the middle of August this year, on the territory covered by the Banja Luka Security Services Centre, there has been increased activity by ever more numerous armed groups which in the last few days has been escalating in scale in the Prnjavor and Bosanska Gradiska area." And further, it says, "Due to the number and diffusion of these groups, the establishment of any kind of control over their activity and the prevention of such activity is becoming an ever more serious security problem through the various illegal actions, in particular the frequent gunfire and gross disturbances of the peace and also recently the perpetration of crimes and violation that seriously threaten the security of citizens and property. These groups are becoming a source of widespread instability and complication of the security situation." And the fourth paragraph starts, "Particularly characteristic is a group of about 30 armed persons in Prnjavor area. Since 11 July, when they returned uniformed and well armed from training in the SAO of Krajina, this group comprised initially of 25 persons mostly from the Kremna, Strpci, Livopoljci and Donji Galjipovci [As interpreted] areas but later joined by a few other persons." And then it goes on "That the most extreme in the activities manifested by this group are, among others, Veljko Milankovic, Slavisa Budak, et cetera. To date the majority of them have had criminal and misdemeanour proceedings brought against them." And on the second page, it goes and it will be the last quotation from this document, "From the very beginning, they have been operating in a calculated and organised way to provoke conflicts and fighting with the active and reserve police force. Shortly after returning, they go around making their presence known, making threats and carrying out organised preparations for an armed attack on the Prnjavor SJB, public security station." And the very last, it's the last paragraph on this second page, "Individually and as a group, they provoke and harass the Muslim population with the aim of precipitating interethnic conflict." You have already -- you have already mentioned this group yesterday, and you stated that you knew Veljko Milankovic. How did you know Veljko Milankovic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My father worked his entire life in the field, particularly in the village of Kremna and the villages around that area. During peace time we met a lot of families there, especially the Milankovic family whom I have known since my youth. I have known Veljko since the time I was city inspector from 1983 to 1987, when a colleague of mine, forestry inspector, submitted several criminal reports against him for cutting down the wood illegally. I know that at the time, Petrovic Miroslav, a policeman, also filed charges against him for an attempt to rape a girl.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In 1991, did you see this group in Prnjavor town?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I have met that group numerous times, also parts of that group, both in the town of Prnjavor and in the village of Kremna where I passed through many times going to the spa called Kulasi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you tell us what kind of uniforms these people wore?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prior to 1991, they mostly walked in grey, olive drab uniforms of the former Yugoslav People's Army. Some of them wore civilian clothes. When the combat started in Croatia and later on in Derventa, they started also wearing camouflage uniforms. Some of them even had a typical blue and white uniform worn by policemen in Knin and SAO Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you see any insignias on their uniforms?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I did see the insignia which was typical also. They had an emblem on one of the sleeves, either right or left one. It was a round emblem with a grey head of a wolf, and there was a text there saying Wolves from Vucjak.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In this report, the villages of Kremna, Strpci, Popovici and Donji Galjipovci are mentioned. What was the ethnicity of people living in these villages?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In Galjipovci, there were mostly Muslims living there. They were the predominant group. And this area is quite close to the town of Prnjavor. The village of Popovici is a peculiar village. It's a Serbian village but it bordered with a Croat village called Kulasi. And the animosity that emerged at the time were probably based on that. As far as the village of Smrtici is concerned, that village borders with the Derventa municipality and it is well known that Croats were the most numerous residents of Derventa. In that area, there are several Bosniak villages around Derventa. One of them is called Omeragici and there are several others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In this report, it says that in 1991, around September, it was a group of about 30 armed persons. Is it correct number for the year 1991?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I am no military expert; however, I believe that that figure could be realistic. A lot of -- I knew a lot of other people who were members of that paramilitary formation because they lived in the municipality of Prnjavor. Later on, I also used to see the other members of that group, the ones who did not originally hail from Prnjavor. At least I didn't Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. know them as coming from Prnjavor. The unit grew with time --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will discuss this later. I just wanted you to make comment on this particular part of the report. This report also discusses the harassment of the Muslim population. Did you see in 1991 or 1992 this group harassing non-Serb population of the Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that that group used to stop all vehicles at checkpoints. They harassed people. They took money away from them also, they confiscated vehicles and other items they had on them. Son of my aunt, they came into his house and confiscated his car - it was a Renault make - and issued him with a receipt, which he has kept until today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you learn or did you know that this group would harassing people in Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I knew that Veljko Milankovic treated very badly some people from the village of Lisinja, according to him this had to do with some pre-war debts. He used to persecute two or three men from that village. Some of them are living in Bihac nowadays. We couldn't hear anything going on, although there was shooting directed at Muslim houses but we didn't leave houses unless we had to go out and do forced labour. If we didn't have to go out and work we stayed at home. We didn't used to frequent coffee bars and taverns.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document also mentions that shortly after returning, they go around making their presence known, making threats and carrying out organised preparation for an armed attack on the Prnjavor Public Security Station. Do you know whether this ever happened, whether this Prnjavor SJB was attacked by this paramilitary formation?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. That paramilitary formation did attack the SJB station in Prnjavor. I was in Prnjavor at the time and I know what was going on in town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know approximately when it happened?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't remember what date it was. I think it was in 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did they succeed?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, they didn't. This is how it went: The police administration in Prnjavor still had a number of professionals among its police force, and at the top of that police station, there were three or four men who were sons of the former commanders of that police station. I will emphasise that those people were true professionals and they tried to take some steps against this group causing trouble in town. This is why the members of the group objected to that. I know that they tried to take the police station. Members of the police administration in Prnjavor put up resistance, as did fathers of them. They came in with hunting rifles and they took positions at the windows of the police station, and it was only by some miracle that there was no shooting there. Several days later, Miroslav Petrovic, a true professional, confiscated two hand grenades from Veljko Milankovic, whereas the other policeman, Tatar, I think his nickname was, arrested several members of that paramilitary formation. It was said at the time that they had been brought to the police administration building.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned now that they arrested some of the members of the -- of this group. After they were arrested, were they charged and convicted of any crimes?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Veljko Milankovic himself was taken into custody and in a way proceedings were instigated against him or rather they attempted to instigate proceedings. A friend of mine from high school and from college, who was a criminal judge in the Court at the time, was in charge of criminal investigation in that case, and immediately after the investigation started, a bomb was placed under her car. She told me that she had received a death threat, threatening her if she continued the investigation. As a professional she wanted to continue investigation. However, she was removed, fired, from the Court and she never returned. She is in private practice now. Following that, Veljko was released from custody.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did they continue --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment, can we have her name, please? If necessary we go into private session.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think we should go to private session.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We go to private session for a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, this group, did they continue in their activities also in 1992? And let's say in the first half of the 1992, was there any attempts to stop their activities?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That group continued being active. I personally am not aware of any attempts to stop their activity. Later on I had an opportunity to see that for myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can I show the witness Exhibit 1790?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This is a document from the 1st Krajina Corps command dated 6 September, 1992, and it is authorisation, "Lieutenant Veljko Milankovic, bearer of identity card number 609/03, Prnjavor, is hereby authorised to collect from you without hindrance the necessary amount of ammunition and Plamen 128 rockets, in particular, for the needs of the 1st Krajina Corps," and it was signed by commander Major General Momir Talic. Did you know whether the group of Veljko Milankovic joined the 1st Krajina Corps?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't have a document or proof to that effect but I know that it actively participated in the combats that were conducted for the purpose of piercing the Posavina corridor with the 1st Corps. They regularly went to a battle field near Derventa, which is located 25 kilometres away from Prnjavor, and I also know that very often, together with other uniformed individuals from the 1st Corps, I presumed, they would bring spoils into the town and transport them further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One moment. I'm going to stop you because you're going beyond what was the substance of the question. I mean you are a lawyer and I don't need to explain this. Please try to limit yourself to answering the question and don't go beyond that. Nothing else, please, because otherwise we would never finish. The question was a very simple one: Are you aware that at any time on or around the date of the 6th September, 1992, Lieutenant Veljko Milankovic formed part of the 1st Krajina Corps? He or his people, his men. Answer yes or no or I don't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. That's it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. I would like to show the witness Exhibit P400.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document is dated 28 of July, 1991. It's from SR BiH Army main staff, and it is signed by Colonel Zdravko Tolimir. The title of this document is, "Report on Paramilitary Formations in the Territory of the Serbian Republic of Bosnia and Herzegovina" and it says, "Paramilitary formations and groups are an important feature of the war in the former Yugoslavia. The paramilitary formations on Serbian Republic of BiH territory have specially identifying names such as Arkan's men, Seselj's men, Captain Dragan's commandos, Captain Oliver's commandos, Charlie's men, Jovic's men, White Eagles, Wolves, Smoke Ribs." My first question is: You already mentioned these wolves. Were you aware of any other Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. paramilitary formations, which would operate on the territory of the Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Are you referring to -- when you say other, apart from the ones that are listed here or particularly the ones that are listed?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yeah. Apart from Wolves, are you aware of any other which are listed in this document, that they would operate on the territory of the Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I think that the Seselj's men were also active there. They searched the houses of the residents of Prnjavor in 1992. They plundered them, mistreated the population. Specially in my street they referred to themselves as Seselj's White Eagles.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, the document I have is not the same as the one that she is referring. To I have a draft translation that's different apparently. The draft translation says the date of the document is 28 July, 1992, and Ms. Richterova said the date of the document she has is 28 July, 1991.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I said 28 July, 1992. I'm sorry, it must have been my mistake. It is 28 July, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. It's page 10, line 17 that says 1991, Your Honour, so we've got that corrected now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. That's no longer a problem. Let's proceed. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm wondering if it might be possible for the Prosecutor to find a copy of the more updated translation for me because there seems to be quite a lot of difference.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. I will provide you with the full translation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richterova. Please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned this group, they called themselves Seselj's. Do you remember what kind of uniform they wore?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They wore uniforms of the Yugoslav People's Army, the olive drab uniforms.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you have opportunity to observe whether this group cooperated with Wolves or whether there were some disputes among -- between them?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Speaking of the event that I mentioned, not only that they didn't cooperate but Vuk's group threw them out of the town and they left for Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The Seselj's left for Derventa or the Wolves?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Seselj's men were already at the front line in the area of Derventa but they entered the town of Prnjavor, they plundered several of our houses and mistreated us. The next day, the Wolves arrested them in a cafe and there were stories to the effect that they had beaten them up and taken them to the border near Derventa. They never returned after that. Or at least I'm not aware of it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, did Wolves arrest them because they were maltreating the Muslims and non-Serb population or what was the reason for their behaviour?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I remember an occasion --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Excuse me, Your Honour, I object to that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I object to that unless there is some reason that he can say that he knows. I mean how could he know what was in their minds when they did that. If there is a foundation, then I won't object.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Please rephrase your question, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you learn the reason why the Wolves arrested the Seselj's?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The next day, after the event, the Wolves' commander met my father and he said that he knew that they had broken into our house. That they had mistreated us --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Let him finish, first, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Please, he's not answering the question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He may be arriving there, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question was simple, not --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he is already partly answering the question.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The question is not what --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, please sit down. Witness, continue with your answer, please. You said, "The next day after the event the wolves' commander met my father and he said that he knew that they had broken into our houses, that they had mistreated us." Please go ahead.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They broke into four or five houses and they even mistreated one Serb family. He said that he had arrested them, that he had beaten them and taken them back to Derventa. The way -- and he said some -- he said to my father something to the effect that there could be no two chiefs in one town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Next question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: On the page 8 of English version, and page 5, B/C/S version, there is a paragraph stating, "The detachment of Veljko Milanovic" - and it will be probably a typo - "from Prnjavor has about 115 men." For the record it is 150. 150. "And is as of recently formally under the command of the 1st KK. Members of this detachment are involved in extensive looting and recently attacked the Tactical Group 3rd command post, arresting one SR BiH Army Colonel in the process." We already discussed your knowledge about the fact whether or not this group was part of the 1st KK. Now I am interested about this looting. Did you see personally that this group would loot -- would be looting on the territory of the Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As I have already indicated, their members confiscated vehicles, tractors, appliances. One of their members confiscated this car that I mentioned. I know what his name is. I can tell you his name. However, most of these goods were transported to the town itself where they were sold or distributed. I was present on an occasion when a member of the Wolves, who is married to Veljko's niece, when he brought 14 cars to a yard next to my house, the complete equipment for a car repair shop and a number of other goods which still had plastic covers on. The same behaviour was observed by many other people whose names I also know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let me intervene a little bit because the substance of the question basically focuses on the word "extensive" looting. Would you say that they were involved in looting generally or in extensive looting? Would you agree with the statement that they were involved in looting in an extensive manner?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what exactly you have in mind when you say looting in an extensive manner but they confiscated everything they could get hold of, timber wood, tractors, trucks, furniture, live stock, home appliances and so on and so forth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: That answers the question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In the previous document, when the report from 1991, there was also mention -- the report mentioned that this group returned from SAO Krajina, from a training. It was in July, approximately July, 1991. Did you know whether this group, underwent any training either in some area of -- some other area of the SAO Krajina or in the Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said yesterday that they went to the SAO Krajina for training. As for Prnjavor, I personally saw huge quantities of cartridges within the compound of the Vucjak agricultural company. I also saw cartridges of hand-held rocket launchers on the ground that they used for training. And this was confirmed to me by the local residents of Krajina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when you said that they found or you personally saw these cartridges, did you know who was -- who was training at that place or you Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. just found these cartridges?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, in this area, in this village, the Vucjak Wolves had their headquarters. The only population living there is Serb. I don't know whether they did this in an organised manner but I know that huge quantities of ammunition were spent there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And if you are saying in this village, and do I not know whether we have it in the transcript, which village are you referring to? Can you tell us the name of the village?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm referring to the village of Kremna, in the Vucjak area, there is a road that turns left in the area leading to the agricultural firm. The area is not inhabited. It is a wooded area and it is well sheltered so they could easily have their training there. There is only a couple stables in the area where they kept horses and the area is located near the Doboj-Prnjavor road.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And now we were talking about this armed group called Wolves. Do you know whether either during the period of time of 1991 or 1992, civilians of Serb ethnicity would be armed?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Many Serb civilians were armed at the time. At the beginning of 1992, in front of the hunter's lodge located some 2 to 3 kilometres outside the town I personally saw a huge trailer truck from which arms were being distributed to the local Serbs. My best friend, a Serb, he fled Prnjavor when they tried to give him a machine-gun by force. He left at that time and never came back.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you non-Serbs, did you try to obtain weapons, either from Serbs or from elsewhere?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I'm not aware of that. I don't know whether anyone in the town of Prnjavor obtained such weapons. I was never offered any weapons but I heard from others that the residents of the Visnja [As interpreted] village located 20 kilometres away from Prnjavor were obtaining some weapons individually. We hunters, we had hunting weapons with legally issued permits, and that's it. That's all we had, as far as the town of Prnjavor is concerned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, when you say the residents of Visnja village, you mean non-Serb residents of Visnja village? Is that correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The village of Visnja is almost 90 per cent Bosniak and it is located some 12 kilometres away from the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think the village is Lisinja not Visnja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I wouldn't know.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Lisinja with a L.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: This is where there was the mosque, something like that.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: The witness agrees that it's Lisinja, the transcript says Visnja but it's Lisinja.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you ever heard any reasons why the Serbs armed themselves?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Serbs claimed that an attack on Prijedor from the direction of Derventa is imminent. They were saying they were arming themselves in order to defend themselves from the Ustashas, referring to the population of Derventa.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I will change subject from arming to something else. Yesterday, and it is in the transcript on page 53, you stated that you were general secretary of the Sloga factory and after you were removed from that organisation, you opened a law firm. Why were you removed from that organisation?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All Bosniaks and Croats were dismissed from work in the period following first multi-party elections, in particular during 1991, if they did not want to go to war in Croatia. Some were dismissed directly. I was, on the other hand, first laid off. That is to say, I was temporarily dismissed, and after that, a relevant decision regarding the termination of employment is adopted. I tried to open a law firm, but unfortunately, it lasted only three days, when it was blown up.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You said that people were -- it happened particularly during 1991 when they didn't want to go to war in Croatia, and you were referring to Bosniaks and Croats. Does it mean that they refused to be mobilised?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them refused to be mobilised - I personally also refused to be mobilised - because they didn't want to go to war against anyone.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And after they refused to be mobilised, what happened? Were they -- did they lose -- did they lose their jobs?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Almost all of them were sacked. Then their apartments, the apartments that they had been given by their companies, were taken away from them. Judicial proceedings were initiated against some of them, including myself, and various types of sanctions were imposed on them. I received -- I had to pay a fine after which I was sent to prison.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: They were sacked. Do you know whether there were any civilian procedures which would be initiated by these Muslims and Croats in respect to their dismissal?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were many people who tried to initiate civil proceedings and press charges. Mostly through a lawyer in Prijedor [As interpreted] whose name was Branislav Maric, who was also one of such victims because he had been dismissed from work at the municipal court for exactly the same reasons. He was the one who represented Croats and Bosniaks in these litigations but I am not aware of any such proceedings ever having been terminated or completed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you say lawyer from Prijedor or from Prnjavor?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Prnjavor, I said Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Thank you, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in 1992, this process of dismissals, did it continue or did it stop?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Dismissals continued, and by the end of the war, almost 90 per cent of Croats and Bosniaks had been dismissed from work and thrown out of their apartments.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In 1991, these people were dismissed because they refused to be mobilised. Do you know the purpose for their dismissal during the 1992?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The reasons were the same. The war was still going on. They needed soldiers, and these call-ups were often repeated.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you also mentioned yesterday that this Dragan Djuric, he often made -- "he often visited local companies to make sure that the remaining Croats and Muslims had been sacked. Two managers complained to me personally that he was doing this on a daily basis." Was it already in 1991 when he went to these companies checking on non-Serb employees? Or was it in 1992 and later?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As early as 1991, he tried to cleanse the Territorial Defence staff of Bosniaks and Croats in order to establish a full control over weapons and documents. Later on, it was the turn of other companies and other work organisations unrelated with the military. People were being dismissed on a daily basis, and even -- he intervened with that objective in mind in companies where such dismissals were not yet taking place.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When we are talking about these dismissals and before we mentioned the SJB in Prnjavor and that they were these professionals who even arrested Milanko Veljkovic, can you tell me at any point --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Veljko Milankovic. I don't know Milan Veljkovic.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sorry, my fault. Veljko Milankovic. Did you know whether at any point the policemen in Prnjavor SJB were dismissed? And I am referring to non-Serb policemen.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very few remained at work. Active policemen were dismissed, as were civilians working in the police administration in Prnjavor. What impressed me most was that three Serb policemen were dismissed as well, who refused to sign the decision on loyalty to the MUP and the new authorities. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yesterday, when we were talking about the release of different parties, and you also mentioned some extreme speeches, you said that it was the time after which incidents started to occur. Which incidents were you referring?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Could you please clarify what period you have in mind?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I am again in my mind period 1991 and 1992, and maybe I can start with you, because you stated that your firm survived only three days and it was destroyed. Did similar things happen on the territory of the Prnjavor town or on the territory of the Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think that these things started taking place in 1991, at the very beginning of that year, in March and April. I tried to record how many sabotage cases there were carried out against privately owned businesses of Muslims and Croats in Prnjavor, but later, it became pointless because some of the facilities were mined up to three times. For example, the business owned by Zenic and there was almost no Muslim or Bosniak businesses remaining who had not been mined. As far as my premises were concerned, they were not completely destroyed, but the windows were broken and damaged and so on. There were more than a hundred such cases in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And these cases of explosions, destruction of premises, did it happen only in 1991 or did it continue in the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I told you that the destruction of facilities in Prnjavor started in 1992, and then continued later on. In 1991, there was shooting at directed those premises because people were going to the battle fields in Knin and Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I know because we have in the transcript that these explosions started in fact in 1991. So now you are stating, and just make it absolutely clear, this -- these explosions and destruction of premises started at the beginning of 1992? Is it correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You also mentioned that Nemanja Vasic, as far as you are concerned, he prevented you from carrying out the referendum in 1992. What happened around the referendum? What was the atmosphere in the Prnjavor town in the time of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He tried to prevent me from carrying out the referendum. The republic committee of Bosnia-Herzegovina appointed me chairman of the referendum committee in Prnjavor. What he succeeded was to limit me to holding referendum in only one building in town, in the culture hall in Prnjavor. However, in four or five villages, we managed to organise the referendum in private homes. People who came to vote at the referendum were provoked and there were threats issued against them but I'm happy that over 800 Serbs participated in the referendum, and some 8.000 people voted for it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell me, in the year 1992, did you notice any checkpoints in either the town of Prnjavor or on the territory of the Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I said that there had been checkpoints in several locations. I, together with European Observer and Mr. Naim Kadic, was stopped on the day the referendum was held. I was stopped by members of that formation at a checkpoint 3 kilometres from the town, on the road leading to the village of Drenova a Croatian village.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Who manned these checkpoints?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally saw Veljko. I came out and explained to him that there was a representative of the international community present there and I told him it would look very bad if he tried to do anything. They returned back to the bunker that had existed there for a year in that location.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And apart from the town -- time of the referendum, did these checkpoints function also later or before the referendum? Or did they set up them only at the time of the referendum?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I claim with certainty that they had been placed there in 1991. I know three or four such checkpoints. I know where they were located and I passed through those checkpoints myself.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And just briefly?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But one moment because these last two questions he didn't answer. The first question was: "Who manned these checkpoints?" and you said "I personally saw Veljko." I suppose Veljko Milankovic you're referring to. But are you not telling us exactly who manned these checkpoints. Was it the Wolves? Was it someone else? Was it the army, the police? Who manned these checkpoints? That was the question.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In that particular case, Veljko Milankovic was there with several of his men.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. And generally, who manned these checkpoints? Was it always the same groups? Or did the groups change?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very frequently, I used to see policemen, members of the police station Prnjavor there, but most often I used to see members of that paramilitary formation. Only on a few occasions in 1991 I saw some people wearing olive drab uniforms there. I assume that they were reservists from Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And the last question, the second question, was directed -- trying to know whether these were checkpoints specifically set up for the purposes of the referendum or whether they were checkpoints that existed before, already.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No. They had not been placed because of the referendum. They had existed there from before.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At the time of the referendum, did you notice any change or changes with regard to these checkpoints? Did they increase in number? Did they remain the same? Were they manned differently?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I did not notice any changes. I think that it remained the same.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you. Madam Richterova, please proceed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you about departure of people from Prnjavor. To your knowledge, in 1991 or 1992, did you see people, non-Serbs, leaving the Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1991, I didn't see them leaving in an organised fashion. Perhaps there had been some individual departures. But as early as 1992, in the second half of it, the so-called organised departures from Prnjavor started.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And what do you mean by "organised departures?" Who organised these departures?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: They were organised by the local authorities, represented by Djordje Stojicic who used to work in the local Red Cross chapter. He used to take 1.000 to 1500 deutschmarks per person departing, whereas the rest of the authorities used to issue certain certificates, naturally for a certain compensation. A person leaving needed to acquire up to seven such certificates. The authorities organised buses. People were loaded into buses and taken to the Hungarian border and left there. I saw dozens of such buses in 1992 and later on.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you say that they needed some certificates, and very briefly, what were they requested to submit if they wanted to leave?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I had to do that myself as well. We had to obtain up to seven various certificates, certifying that we were allowed to leave because we were not fit for military service. Then we had to get a certificate that we cancelled our telephone account, electricity account, that we had paid our water bill and so on. Various other certificates were needed if people needed -- if people had been issued with various items. My nephew, who was four year old, also needed to get a certificate saying that he was not fit for military service. We had to pay several hundred deutschmarks in order to be issued such certificates, and upon presenting these certificates, we were allowed to board the bus.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness document called, "Authorisation." This document was provided by the witness upon his arrival, and I would like him to make a comment on this. I provided Your Honours with the copy as well as the counsel. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have it, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I can provide you with extra copy, if you wish but at least confirm that I gave you the copy yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, it was given to me and I somehow left it at my flat. I did have it and Ms. Richterova is perfectly rightly --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Usher, all right. Okay. Yes, Madam Richterova.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: This document is from 1994 but I would like to ask you whether what is stated in this document, and I'm going to read it, also relates to the year 1992, if you know. And it says, in the middle, "I hereby authorise him" he's referring to above-named lawyer, "to sell the above-mentioned property, transfer it to any other individual of his choosing or exchange it within six months of the attestation of this authorisation at the Prnjavor Basic Court. In case he does not sell or exchange the above mentioned property within six months of the attestation of this authorisation the above-mentioned real estate shall become the public property and ownership of the Prnjavor Municipal Assembly."

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, to your knowledge, was this practice in 1992 as well or only in 1994?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That applied from 1992 until the end of the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was it easy to sell such a property in 1992 and it would mean that you would obtain money from the lawyer or whoever bought this property?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, it was almost impossible to sell property because the Serb residents were obtaining property from local authorities free of charge. They used to put up many people in our houses en masse, and those who considered themselves lucky managed to sell their property for a ridiculously low sums. For example, for 2.000 German marks. I know some people who bought such Bosniak's or Croat houses for a ridiculously low price. This certificate was the mother of all certificates, and one had to get this one first.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And if you didn't have this certificate, did you have to sign over -- sign over your property in some other way?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Without this certificates, we were unable to depart. There were cases where individuals signed over their property to Serb residents. Some have returned their property since and some have not. Those wishing to depart signed over the ownership free of charge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I want to ask you whether you heard about any announcement asking either non-Serbs or all the Prnjavor population to hand over illegally and legally owned weapons?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not only there were various declarations and announcements, but searches had been carried out in many houses. They were looking and confiscating -- looking for and confiscating weapons. They were looking for hunting rifles as well, and were confiscating various equipment that had been issued to military conscripts previously. There were many such searches.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Before you proceed, Judge Janu?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes. I would like to go back to this authorisation. Madam Richterova, could you please clarify for the Chamber if this authorised lawyer, Branislav Slav Malic was a person who was chosen by the witness himself or was it somebody officially appointed for this business?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, you heard the question of the Judge Janu. Can you please answer it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: We chose ourselves the attorney to whom we would give power of attorney. Any attorney could have drafted a power of attorney of this kind, but most of the Bosniaks gave a power of attorney to the attorney they considered to be the most honest.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Yes. That's what I wanted to know.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I will take advantage of this and I would like to tender this document into evidence, and it would be Exhibit P1766.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And I would like to ask you one more question about these departures. Can you just briefly tell us, if you know, what made these people to leave? To leave the municipality of Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was the pressure that these people were subjected to on a daily basis, and also it was economically non-viable for them to remain there. All of the people who had been dismissed from work lost their income, medical insurance, health insurance. Following that, they would be evicted from their homes into the street, and they had no other choice but go where they could, and they could only go via Serbia and Hungary to the western countries.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you. Before this question, I asked you about the announcement to surrender weapons, and you stated there were various announcements. Can you be more specific whether these announcements were to surrender legally obtained weapons, illegally obtained weapons, and whether these announcements were made -- were asking non-Serbs or all the population?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The announcements were always addressed to the non-Serb residents. In my bag here, I have a certificate on confiscating of hunting rifles from my father and brother, and a pistol, Bereta make, from me. These certificates were written by hand and confiscation was carried out by regular police from Prnjavor. No hunting weapons were confiscated from Serb residents at all.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, only the first sentence of your reply answers the question. The rest was not asked from you. The question was whether the announcements were made -- were directed, in other words, only to non-Serbs or all the population. And you said always addressed to the non-Serb residents, full stop. The rest, the certificates, we are not interested in, unless you are specifically asked about them. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now I would like to ask you about the religious buildings in the territory of the Prnjavor. Were there mosques in these four villages you mentioned as purely Muslim villages?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: There were five mosques.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you state in which places, in which villages or towns, these mosques were?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: One was in the town itself. It was called the City Mosque. One was in the village of Lisnja, one in the village of Puraci, one in Konjuhovci village and the last one was in Galjipovci village. To avoid confusion, that village is sometimes called Mravica but it's one and the same village, Galjipovci and Mravica.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I would like to show the witness Exhibit P1788, and 1789. And I would start with the 88. The first document is dated 22nd of June, 1992, and it says, "An Islamic place of worship in Prnjavor has been demolished." Do you know whether at this time the mosque in Prnjavor was demolished or damaged?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know that the mosque was targeted twice. On the first occasion, it was damaged, and on the second one, it was razed to the ground. I couldn't tell you the dates but at any rate, it was targeted by terrorists twice.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And at any of these occasions, did you see it personally when it was damaged or did you learn it from someone else?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I personally saw the damage. Both times, I came to see the mosque, because my ancestors are buried right next to the mosque and I wanted to make sure that their graves had not been damaged. So I saw the condition the mosque was in on both occasions.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And did you -- do you know or did you know at the time who did it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I can't make any claims but there were rumours in town to the effect that the first damage was caused by Ranko Milanovic. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I object to what the rumours were in town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Objection sustained.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to show the witness the second document, 1789.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It says, "All places of worship not belonging to the Serbian Orthodox Church are being demolished in the Prnjavor areas." To your knowledge, which mosques or other religious buildings, Muslim religious or Catholic religious building were demolished or damaged during the year 1992?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I know which ones were destroyed but I can't give you the dates. In 1992, the mosque in Puraci was blown up. The mosque in Lisnja was also damaged in 1992 by shelling and torching. Mosque in Konjuhovci was blown up in 1994. Whereas I could not remember the date when the mosque in Galjipovci was mined. I think that in 1992, the Catholic church in Kulasi was damaged and one house of worship, a chapel, in the place called Karaci.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We need to stop here. Now, Mr. Ackerman and Madam Richterova, how much longer do you think you require to finish?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I am more or less done but I reserve to the last word after the break but 99 per cent I am done, and so the witness will be in Mr. Ackerman's hands.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In other words, when we resume, do you anticipate you require more time or not?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: No, no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Ackerman, if we resume in 15 minutes' time, how much time do you require? I'm asking you more or less to see whether we should hold the meeting at 5.00 or whether we should delay the meeting until after 5.00? I would rather prefer to finish first with the witness and then have the meeting rather than have the meeting and then come back to the courtroom, continue with the cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'll finish as quickly as I can but I'm guessing I have an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You have an hour and a half.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I may do it faster than that but that's a guess.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Would you agree with us that it's wiser to finish the witness before we meet.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think Ms. Korner will be delayed a bit anyhow so that probably works.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So do I take it that a break of 15 minutes would suffice? So we will break now for 15 minutes, resuming at 5 past 4.00, and then the understanding is that we proceed with the cross-examination until we finish the cross-examination. And that means that someone from your bench, Madam Richterova, needs to contact Ms. Korner to inform her that the meeting that we have scheduled for 5.00 will probably start at about 5.30 instead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. It will be done.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Thanks.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm sorry, Your Honour, but I have a few more questions, if you allow me.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I was pretty sure you would have. Yes, go ahead.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, were there any collection centres in the Prnjavor municipality in 1992?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In 1992, after the events in Lisnja, a collection centre was established in the town itself, within the compound of the shoe factory, Sloga, and then another 1, 2 kilometres outside the town, in silos of the local mill.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And do you know who were the people who were taken to these camps?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: This collection centre which was located in the town was intended for the men that had been taken away from the Lisnja village. As for the collection centre in the silo, SDA activists and a number of people from Derventa were detained there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You mentioned now after the events in Lisnja. Can you very briefly tell us what happened in the village of Lisnja?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The village of Lisnja came under an attack in mid-1992. The attack was perpetrated by the members of the then military, I don't know whether it was the JNA or the VRS, and paramilitary -- the paramilitary formation, Wolves from Vucjak. I was not present during the attack but a few days later I passed through the village and I saw that 54 houses had been burned down, five or six people were killed in this first attack, four of them from the Halilovic family, all men were detained in the collection centre in Prnjavor.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, do you know whether, during the year of 1992, some other villages on the territory of Prnjavor were also attacked by either the JNA or the Serb army or whether the Lisnja was the only village?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: With Their Honours' permission, I'll try to explain. There were only four villages located along the road leading to Prnjavor. Two were Bosniak villages and two were Croat villages. All these villages were attacked and partly burned down. People, that is the residents, were captured and detained in camps. Others were expelled from their homes. Again, those villages were Bosniak villages and Croat villages, Kulasi and Dragalovci.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And Mr. Odobasic, how did you know that these villages were attacked? How did you learn about that?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As for the events in Lisnja and Puraci, I personally talked to a number of people because I had friends there, and as regards the villages of Kulasi and Dragalovci I was later taken to perform forced labour in those villages and I was able to see the damage done to the houses and the church in Kulasi.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You just mentioned forced labour or work obligation. When was work obligation established in the Prnjavor municipality?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: As regards me and my group, we were taken there in September and October, in 1992.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And was work obligation established before or were you the first group?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I cannot answer that question. I'm not aware of that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you -- you stated you started performing this forced labour from September, 1992. Just briefly, what did you do as a part of work obligation?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My group had specific tasks. It consisted of 14 intellectuals and former leaders, local leaders. We were taken to Serb villages where we were made to clear ditches, repair roads, cut firewood. Later, we also were taken to the fish ponds and clear the area over there. Some people were made to work for a certain Bogdan Neimarevic, fire or six people went to his house. They wanted to show us to the local village population. They transferred us from one location to another.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you left the municipality of the Prnjavor in 1994; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Before you left, you were arrested and detained? Just please confirm whether it is correct that you were arrested and detained in 1994.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was arrested on two occasions in 1994.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in which detention centre you were held?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was not held in any of the detention centres. I was taken to the local police station where I was beaten up. And would then be thrown out, outside the police station, and left there to fend for myself. I spent two and a half years working in fish ponds that really looked like real prison camps.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In -- I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, there is some confusion. Page 35, starting at line 6, somewhere in that answer he said, line 35, 8, the words two years later should be in there. I think where it says later, I think what he said was two years later, we also were taken to the fish ponds. That's what has been suggested to me by my assistant.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What we have here is this.. We were taken to Serb villages where we were made to clear ditches, repair roads, cut firewood. Later, we also were taken to the fish ponds. When you said later, did you say just later or did you say two years later?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] After September, we were kept there for about two months in the area of those roads, and until the 3rd of June, 1994, my group was taken often to the fish ponds. It was only on several occasions that we were taken elsewhere to clean the roads from snow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. All right. Thank you, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And in 1996, you became a member of state commission for tracing the missing persons; is it correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Correct.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And can you tell us very briefly what was your role in this institution?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: My objection is we are talking about 1996. I can't see how it's relevant to anything in this indictment what his role was with that commission in 1996.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: What is the reason for your question?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The reason for my question is because of his function within this institution is relevant to exhumations and I want it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Objection overruled. Proceed with the answer, Witness, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] From the 1st of April, 1996, I've been a member of the state commission for tracing missing persons. I was also the deputy president of that commission. For a while.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What is the main purpose of this institution, of this commission?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is still its purpose to trace missing persons. The persons who went missing in Bosnia and Herzegovina in -- during the war.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you also collect information regarding exhumations, regarding findings of graves on the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Throughout this period of time, I've been collecting information on mass graves in the territory of Bosnia and Herzegovina. However, most of the time I spent collecting information on exhumations of mass and individual graves discovered in the area of Bosnian Krajina, that is in the western part of Bosnia.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And to your knowledge, how many exhumations took place in the area of the Autonomous Region of Krajina in which you participated?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My team that has been working since 1996 exhumed more than 3.000 victims in 15 various locations, that is in 104 mass graves. Five of them were major ones. The biggest one contained 374 bodies. 35 per cent of the -- 55 per cent of the bodies were identified.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And only, if you could answer my previous question, did you participate in all exhumations or in what was the percentage of exhumations in which you participated?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think I personally -- I personally participated in 80 per cent of these exhumations and I was the leader in many of them and was working with the local investigating judge.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Odobasic, this concludes my examination-in-chief of this witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I thank you, Madam Richterova. Mr. Ackerman, before you start, because I think we need to deal with this with some urgency, I understand you have been served now with a copy of Prosecution's interparties justification for an ex parte filing.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, I've seen it, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have -- let's go into private session, first of all.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Let me get my copy.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: And Mr. Ackerman will start with his cross-examination. Now, go ahead, I don't need to tell -- to say anything to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour I think now that I'm not going to finish by 5.30. I don't know what Your Honours pleasure is. I think we probably should go ahead and break at 5.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: We have these options, Mr. Ackerman, because as you can imagine, although we started at 2.15, we are -- the three of us have had a meetings this morning and I in particular had meetings even before I had meetings with the other two judges so there is a limit to which we can continue. The position is as follows, however, that tomorrow morning, at 9.30, I have a Status Conference and then at 10.30, I have another Status Conference. Now, these two Status Conferences will roughly last maximum until 11.15, 11.30, I anticipate, so if you think that we could still meet tomorrow at 11.15 or 11.30 instead of this evening, after we finish with this -- I wouldn't like to have the cross-examination interrupted, if possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't mind that and I'd prefer that frankly.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But we need to see whether Ms. Korner is -- can live with that. I mean whether it's convenient for her.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I would really like to meet at 5.30 if we can, unless that's totally inconvenient to Your Honours

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But he won't finish --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: He can come back tomorrow. He's answered questions he's not been asked so it's his fault if he's still here tomorrow.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In that case, we it actually stop at 5.00 and have the meeting at 5.00 and dedicate the all the time required for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think 5.30 would be the best time which would enable Ms. Korner to settle down for the meeting because she's still somewhere on her way.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. 5.30 we stop for the meeting.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right. Thank you, Your Honours. Cross-examined by Mr. Ackerman:

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, I want you to look at the document that's now been marked P1766.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Before you proceed, until when was the witness scheduled or planned to remain here in The Hague?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think he was scheduled to stay -- to finish today but maybe we can ask the witness whether he has some other commitments and I really do not know his plans.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I'm told that his planned departure is within a couple of days. Within a couple of days.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I didn't have this information so ...

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Were you planned to stay in The Hague tomorrow or were you planned to leave The Hague tomorrow?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, I was told that I should remain here for four days, and this expires tonight. I have been given four per diems and this is what was told to me. However, this is true that I also requested to stay one additional day.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: One additional day, to your own expense or at the expense of the Tribunal?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] At the expense of the Tribunal, in order to arrange certain other things and documents unrelated to this particular case.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was informed that lawyers from other team want to contact Mr. Odobasic as well, and in fact they are waiting for us to finish because until now, they didn't -- they haven't had the opportunity to contact him.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The reason why I'm saying this is that I'm being informed by the Registrar that his departure from The Hague is planned for Friday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So -- I can check this information and come to you as soon as possible.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. In the meantime, please start, Mr. Ackerman, sorry to have interrupted you.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: No problem, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, I was a little bit abrupt in starting my cross-examination of you. I think the Judge told you my name is John Ackerman, I represent Mr. Brdjanin. And I have a few things I want to discuss with you. And the first of those is this document that you brought with you to the Tribunal, this authorisation dated 13 June, 1994. It authorises a lawyer by the name of Branislav Malic to deal with your real estate. What is the ethnicity of Branislav Malic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He's a Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What in fact was done with this authorisation? What happened to your property?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After I left the town, I sent a letter to Mr. Malic, whereby I withdrew the power of attorney that I had given to him. In the meantime, he had made no attempts to sell my property.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you still own the property?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did Branislav Malic stay there then throughout the war?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: He lived -- he stayed there at the same address, and he still lives there.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Why is it that you left and he stayed? How did that happen?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Your Honours, in order to answer the question of the Defence counsel, I should like to be given several photographs to show to Mr. Ackerman. So if the usher could perhaps show me these photographs and I will be able to answer Mr. Ackerman's question.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You understand my question is fairly simple. Why did you leave and why did he stay?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I suppose he can tell us only why he left, because what's good for the goose is good for the gander, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I think I'll change the question. Let me do that.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's the case, isn't it, that you left of your own accord so as to sort of better your situation in life? Or to try to?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That's not true.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So is it your position that you were forced to leave?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The fee for this document, this authorisation, was 11 dinars. Do you have any idea how much that was in deutschmarks in June of 1994?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't tell you now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: A few pennies, I would imagine a few pfennigs, something insignificant.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Lets than ten pfennigs, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. I told you I don't remember what the exchange rate was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So you have absolutely no memory of what dinars were worth in terms of deutschmarks in Prnjavor in 1994; is that what you're telling us?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't remember, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That's fine. I can't expect to you remember something you don't remember. Do you know a person by the name of Goran Stokanovic?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Goran Stokanovic, no, I have no recollection of that name.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Let me give you some more information about Goran Stokanovic. He was the son of Ranko born 12 August, 1961 in Prnjavor. Does that help [Realtime transcript read in error "represent"] You?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The transcript says that does that represent you? I heard Mr. Ackerman say, "Does that help you?"

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: That's what I said, Your Honour. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you ever visit the Gostovici detention camp?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Never.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: If Goran Stokanovic says in a statement that he saw you when you visited there, that Jasmin Odobasic from Prnjavor visited that camp, he would be incorrect?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Can you state, please, which year he was supposed to visit the camp?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Well, the question I asked was did he ever visit the camp and his answer is no. Was there a year, sir, in which you did visit the camp? Did you visit the camp, for instance, in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Just put a plain, straightforward question, Mr. Ackerman. Did he ever visit the camp, from 1990 onwards, 1991 onwards.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think I did that and I think he said no.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But I think it's the only way of bringing this to an end.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'll ask you again, sir: Did you ever visit that camp at Gostovici?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know any camp near Gostovic and I never visited any such camp.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know anything about the Zenica KPD correction centre?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was the state prison before the war, during the war, and is that today.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Did you visit there in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you recall --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: May I ask you the relevance of your question now that we are in 1995, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'll move on, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Prnjavor is located about 50 kilometres from the Croatian border, is it not?

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And before the multi-party elections, before there were these various parties, I think you say that life in that municipality was very friendly and peaceful; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Very peaceful and harmonious.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You gave a statement to the Prosecutors which I'd ask that you have to consult, dated 30 January, 1999. Before I ask you a question about that, in this municipality, where there was this harmony and everything was friendly and peaceful, how was it that there were villages that were basically 100 per cent Muslim and villages that were basically 100 per cent Serb and why was it people were unwilling to live together if there was this kind of harmony and friendship and peacefulness?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't understand your question entirely but I will answer, Mr. Ackerman. These regions have been --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
