utterances.text: Wait a minute, please don't answer a question you don't understand. If you don't understand a question, ask me to clarify it because then your probably not answering --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Clarify it, I don't think it needs much clarification but please do make an effort and clarify it, Mr. Ackerman, make things simpler to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The question I'm trying to ask you, sir, is this: You say that -- you tell us that before the multi-party situation developed, that life in that municipality was friendly and peaceful and that there were a lot of mixed marriages, things of that nature. What I want to know is why is it in that climate people continued to bunch together in ethnic communities so that there were communities of exclusive Muslims, communities of exclusive Serbs and that sort of thing? Why was that if there was all this harmony? Do you understand now?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, there was no ethnically pure environment there. The population was mixed, and that situation was inherited from the times going back 200 to 300 years.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So these villages that you talked about as being Serb villages and Muslim villages really were mixed villages? Is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was mixed but of course the percentages varied. If I said Muslim village, then I meant the village predominantly populated by Muslims and the same goes for Serb or Croat villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So like, for instance, this village I think it was called Kremna or something like that, where Milankovic's group first started operating, that would have been a village that was primarily Serb but contained a large number of Muslims?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It was populated mostly by Serbs and very few Muslims. The number of Muslims was minimal.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Minimal being how many, would you think?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I couldn't give you a figure. I know that there were several families living in state-owned housing. There was a Muslim family living there, and there were several mixed marriages. So the number was very few indeed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In your statement to the Prosecutor, it's the one, two, three, four, fifth paragraph of that statement, it says that you said this: "Starting in 1980, all nationalities had their own schools and cultural societies." True?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Most of them did have it.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So the Muslims went to Muslim schools, the Croats went to Croat schools, the Serbs went to Serb schools and each of those groups had their own cultural society; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. That's not correct. It's not true that Muslims went to Muslim schools and Serbs went to Serb groups. These three groups all spoke Serbo-Croat and they went to the same schools. What I said applied to Italians. Italians had their own schools. The Czechs and Ukrainians had their own schools and as far as the cultural societies are concerned, the Ukrainians had their own, it was called Taras Sevcenko. The Czechs had their own cultural society, as did Italians. In Lisnja, in the Muslim environment, there was a cultural society as well, and the one in town had members coming from all ethnic backgrounds.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I think you explained that. When you said all nationalities in your statement, you didn't mean the Serbs or the Croats or the Muslims; right?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: At that time, they were considered peoples, whereas the rest were ethnic minorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. Thank you. I understand now. You told us yesterday that the SDS didn't have much of a following in the town of Prnjavor itself but found its support in various surrounding villages, correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. I said so. It is correct and that's exactly how it was.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You told us about a time when Karadzic came to the area to hold a SDS rally, this being the rally where you say Dusan Zelenbaba spoke of Serbs selling cows and buying guns. This clearly was a rally that was held prior to the multi-party elections, was it not?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: All of the rallies were held before the multi-party elections. One day before the elections themselves there is a ban on all political speeches. It is called the pre-election silence.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: What you told us about it yesterday, and this is -- Ms. Richterova, I'm not going to be able to give you a page number. I can give you a time signature, 17.22.17. You were asked about when this ideal life that you had been talking about changed, and your answer was as follows, sir: "It happened with the formation of national political parties. This harmonious life started to change and I remember that it came as a big surprise which was followed by fear in Prnjavor, when in 1989, at a rally organised by the SDS, a certain Mr. Zelenbaba declared, `citizens you better start selling your livestock and start buying rifles and getting ready for war.' People were shocked and then incidents started to occur." So that's what you told us yesterday; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Should I answer.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: My question was, that's what you told us yesterday; correct?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Mr. Odobasic, could you please answer that question?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I've said yes twice.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: But it didn't show up in the transcript. Before you proceed, Mr. Ackerman, just out of curiosity but isn't the family name Zelenbaba a Muslim surname?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I think it's a Serb originally from Knin Krajina.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Sir, it's not possible, is it, that there could have been a SDS rally anywhere in Bosnia-Herzegovina in 1989, since the SDS party was not even created until July of 1990, was it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: It is possible that I made a mistake. However, there were some other smaller rallies in Prnjavor. Yesterday I said that I couldn't remember the date of that particular meeting -- rally, but I'm sure that it was held prior to multi-party elections in Bosnia and Herzegovina.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, so am I. And the only rally I'm talking to you about right now, we will talk about some others in a moment, the only one I'm talking about right now is the one where Karadzic was president -- was present and Dusan Zelenbaba made this statement. Where was that rally held? Which of these outlying villages where the SDS was able to acquire some support? Which of those villages was it in which this rally was held?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The rally I spoke about was held in town at the central square in front of the department store called Prima. And as far as your second question is concerned, I think -- I'm not 100 per cent sure but I think that there were some 30 villages predominantly populated by Serbs around the Prnjavor area. I'm not sure in which villages exactly rallies were held but I'm sure they were held in larger villages.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: But didn't you tell us yesterday that rallies were not held in Prnjavor itself because the SDS couldn't get any support? They had to hold their rallies in the various villages? Did I misunderstand you yesterday?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: You misunderstood me yesterday. I said that the rallies of the SDS and SDP were held at the city square. The rally of the SDA was held in Lisnja, and I repeated that twice yesterday.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: All right. This statement that was made by Dusan Zelenbaba, that was made, wasn't it, in the context of there being a war going on in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know what Zelenbaba meant and what was the context of his statement. However, it sounded very dangerously.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Well, there was a war going on in Croatia at the time, wasn't there?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: If you say so.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know that or not? I mean you're the one that's testifying, not me?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know, sir.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, you talked about rallies of other parties. Did you attend -- how many of these rallies did you actually attend? Did you attend any HDZ rallies or SDA rallies?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: HDZ did not have a chapter in Prnjavor, and as far as I know, it did not hold any rallies. As far as attending other rallies, I only once attended the SDA rally in Lisnja as an observer of my party, the SDP. They sent five invitations to the SDP party and our leadership designated five of us who were to attend that rally.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, at that SDA rally, there were symbols displayed, were there not, things like Islamic flags, things of that nature?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: First of all, you have to explain what you mean when you say Islamic flags.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Well, flags with the crescents and the star, similar to the flag from Iran?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I did not see such flags at that rally. However, I saw a large number of green and white flags with the SDA written on them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I want to go back to your statement now. After the elections had taken place, you say the SDS replaced all the general managers and directors who were not Serbs, as well as all Serbs who were not members of the SDS; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I did not say replaced. I said removed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: So they weren't any replacements, these were just jobs that ended?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. There were people there who had just started working and then were dismissed.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The language of your statement, sir is this, and it could be an error but what it says in your statement is this: "The SDS replaced all general managers and directors who were not Serbs. As well as all Serbs who were not members of the SDS." So according to this, you did use the word "replaced".

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Now, when you say the SDS replaced these people, you mean the SDS authorities who were elected after the first multi-party elections that were won by the SDS party, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I will explain. I will explain, Mr. Ackerman. The SDS won absolute majority, and the most important offices in town were filled by their people. However, other people who in a way could have presented an obstacle to their policy were removed from office. For example my school friend, Esad Mesic [As interpreted] who was a plain warehouser in the TO warehouse, that had weapons there, was dismissed. Vjekoslav Blazevic, a chief of TO staff was dismissed because he was a Croat. Salko Corakovic was removed because he was not loyal, as were others, and I can give you names of people who held important offices who were dismissed as well as those who held plain jobs but were dismissed as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I'm not disagreeing with you about whether there were dismissals, sir, maybe you misunderstood me. What I'm trying to find out from you is who it was that was responsible for these people being dismissed and I suggested to you that it was the elected leaders of the SDS who had been elected in the election. Now, is that correct or is that not correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Naturally. The leader or one of the leaders of the SDS was the most active one in inspecting and ensuring dismissals.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And these persons who were replaced were persons who did not adhere to the SDS platform and philosophy regardless of whether they were Serb, Muslim or Croat; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, most of these people were apolitical, they had nothing to do with politics. They didn't even know what a SDS platform meant. Their misfortune was the fact that they were Croats, Bosniaks and others.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: The others were Serbs who were not members of SDS that were dismissed too, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course, the lawyer that I mentioned, Branko Malic who was thrown out of the Court, was a Serb, and then eight police officers, including Mr. Petrovic, a number of directors at the Prnjavor Radio, Mr. Nedjeljko Sanco who was a Serb. I can give you the names of a few other people as well.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: When did you first go to work for the shoe factory?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: In late 1987.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And when you went to work for the shoe factory, was it required that you be a member of a particular party?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The new parties were not yet established in 1987.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were a member of the Communist Party in 1987 or you couldn't have held that job; right?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I was for two years, from 1987 until the first multi-party elections, two years and a half. Prior to that, I had never been a member of the League of Communists.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I wouldn't have become one if --

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Go ahead, finish your answer. You wouldn't have become one if what?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: My family was basically anti-communist. I never wanted to join the League of Communists. In 1987, 1987, when I held a different position, a different job, my position was in jeopardy and that is why I joined the League of Communists, and -- but apart from that, I already carried out some important functions and held some important offices within the town as a result of my professional qualifications.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And it's the case, isn't it, that for years -- I think, sir, that I'm told that you said in answer to my question that you -- that you joined the Communist Party because you were told that you could lose your job if you didn't do that. Is that what you told us?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: That just didn't make it into the transcript and that's why I had to ask you again. We have to also watch the transcript and make sure things get there. And that was a system that had existed in Yugoslavia for years and years and years, that to hold important positions in state enterprises, one needed to be a member of the League of Communists? That's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Not in every case. Between 1981 and 1987 I was not a member of the League of Communists and yet I held important positions in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: How about when you -- but when you went to work for the shoe factory, that was the time you were told you could lose the job if you were not a member of the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. You misunderstood me. It was not at that time.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Tell me when it was.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: After 1985, while I was the chief inspector in the town.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: All right. When the multi-party elections were held, instead of the Communist Party being in charge, demanding that people be members of the Communist Party to hold these positions, the SDS party took power and they made the same demand, and it didn't have anything to do with whether you were Muslim, Croat and Serb, it had to do with whether you were a member of the SDS and adhered to their philosophy, didn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, SDS was a one-nation, one single ethnic party so you cannot really compare the two.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is it your position that there were no non-Serbs who were members of SDS?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I think he has already answered that question, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I just want to make sure it's clear, Your Honour, that that's his position.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: He doesn't need to answer the question, because it's clear enough.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: So Your Honour's position is that when he said one, single ethnic party, that that's the answer to that question?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: All right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not the answer. He has already stated that there were Serbs who were not members of the SDS, who were given the sack. So there were -- doesn't affect the SDS from being what he has described it to be.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The fact that you have members of the same ethnicity not belonging to that party doesn't mean that that party can't be mono-ethnic.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I understand that, Your Honour. I just want to find out from him if it's his position that there were no non-Serbs that were members of SDS.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Answer the question, Mr. Odobasic.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ackerman, I didn't say, and I don't know, whether there were any non-Serbs in SDS. I didn't have any insight. I didn't have any access to the SDS. I don't know. You can check that information. But I know that most of the members, in most of the cases, the membership was exclusively Serb.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: There was a division going on in Bosnia-Herzegovina between those people who were in favour of independence and that was primarily people who had voted in the referendum for independence, and those who were opposed to independence and wanted to remain part of Yugoslavia, and it turned out that most of those in favour of independence were non-Serb and most of those against it were Serb, that's true, isn't it?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It isn't true, Mr. Ackerman.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Why don't you tell us what your interpretation of the division regarding independence or not was? What's untrue about what I just suggested to you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: The untrue is what you said that there were no Serbs who supported the independence of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I said out of 8.000 people who voted in favour, approximately 800 Serbs turned out. They had serious problems. Some were turned back from the voting places, but in spite of all this torture and abuse, they did vote in favour of Bosnia and Herzegovina. I'm speaking of therefore not only Croats and Bosniaks but also of some Serbs, and a number of other minorities.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes. Your question must not have been properly interpreted to you because my question contained the word "most" of the Serbs and most of the non-Serbs, not all of them, and you agree with me that most of the Serbs were opposed to independence and most of the non-Serbs were in favour of it, but not all, in either case?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Mr. Ackerman, 66 per cent of people turned out for the referendum in Bosnia and Herzegovina, which is a much higher percentage than the percentage of Croats and Bosniaks in Bosnia and Herzegovina. Therefore many Serbs turned out but I cannot speculate as to their exact number.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: I understand that. I'm not arguing with you about that. I think you've answered my question and I appreciate it. Now, I want to talk to you about mobilisation. You discussed it in your statement. When the mobilisation was announced, it applied to everyone, didn't it? It meant Bosniaks, Croats, as well as Serbs?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And people were dismissed from their work who refused to respond to the mobilisation; correct?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, in a significant number of cases.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And again, that wasn't something that depended on whether they were Muslim, Croat or Serb but whether they responded to the mobilisation. So Serbs who failed to respond to the mobilisation were treated the same and dismissed from their positions also, weren't they?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. You will have to check that. Except for the cases that I mentioned.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You know that the Bosniaks didn't respond because Alija Izetbegovic, the President of Bosnia-Herzegovina, said that Bosniaks should not respond to mobilisation. You know that, don't you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Of course.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And even in the face of that, some Bosniaks did in fact respond to the mobilisation and became part of the army, didn't they?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And they weren't dismissed and they didn't lose their apartments, were -- did -- were they?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: It's true that they weren't? They were not.

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, yes, that's what I said.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: And you yourself -- I think you told us earlier you refused to be mobilised and were actually prosecuted for that, weren't you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Do you know about or did you hear about any Serbs who were prosecuted for failing to respond to mobilisation?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. I didn't hear about them.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: In your statement on page 6, referring to the same statement, you said that the last Bosniak was expelled from Prnjavor in 1995. Now, by that time, you weren't there yourself, were you?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: You were still in Prnjavor in 1995?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. You say the last Bosniak was expelled from Prnjavor in 1995. That's what you --

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Except for those who were loyal or the representatives of the Army of Republika Srpska.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Okay. When you say expelled, what do you mean?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Sir, in a large number of cases, until this last wave of persecutions in 1991, people had been brutally beaten, mistreated, maimed and made to leave. I should perhaps show you a document and tell you how me and my family, what we looked like at the time we were expelled. The last departure took place in 1995, and it included several thousands of people. It was organised by local authorities because a military action was going on in the SAO Krajina and Serb refugees were coming in and they were being accommodated in the houses of the people who were being expelled. I met several hundred of such people in Zenica. I took care of them and provided accommodation for them in 1995.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Is it your contention before this Court that you yourself were being expelled?

utterances.speaker: JASMIN ODOBASIC [Resumed]
utterances.text: Once again, Your Honours, I would like to be allowed to show the document which will prove that I was expelled from the town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: You are free to show us whatever you like, Mr. Odobasic, and then we decide whether it's relevant or not. But if you have a document which you would like to show us in relation to the question that you are being asked or the series of questions that you are being asked now, you are free to do that.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] If I can please have the assistance of the usher? If he can take the document.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Mr. Odobasic, yes, while you hand these documents to the usher, if you would tell us whether these documents that you intend to show us, whether you had showed them to anyone else before you came here or since you have been here?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Can you please explain who do you have in mind when you say anyone else?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: I have in mind investigators of the Tribunal or members of the team for the Prosecution of the Tribunal. Did you make them aware of these documents? Did you show them these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I handed them over to the investigative organs of Bosnia and Herzegovina and I'm not aware of whether they have been forwarded to the Office of the Prosecutor.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Okay. So let's see what documents you would like us to see. First, I would like to have them brought to us so that we have a look before --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. Usher, please show them to Madam Richterova and to Mr. Ackerman. Mr. Ackerman now.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I'd like to know if Ms. Richterova has seen these before.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. I saw these pictures and I was informed that these are results of Mr. Odobasic's beating in 1994, and because we were dealing with the events in 1992, I informed Mr. Odobasic that we cannot use them.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Do you have anything else to state, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I'm concerned with his answer that he'd never shown them to the Prosecution, Your Honour. That obviously is not true, and even one of his statements --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Well --

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: -- indicates that he showed them to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: It's not incompatible with what he has stated because if they had been given to the authorities in Bosnia-Herzegovina, and then in turn those authorities handed them over to the Prosecution, that's perfectly compatible.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: But it's not compatible with his statement of 15 March, 1999, to the Office of the Prosecutor, where he says, "I am providing copies of 17 photographs which I and my brother took of injuries myself, my brother, my father and my brother's wife received." So when he told us today he'd not given these to the Prosecutor before, I just think that's not a correct statement.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you provide us with an explanation, Mr. Odobasic? Because it seems that in March of 1999, when you were interviewed by the Office of the Prosecutor, you handed photos. Were these photos included among those?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It is about these photos as well, but I personally didn't hand them over at that time.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Okay. These photos represent what? First of all, is what Madam Richterova stated, that they refer to beatings allegedly sustained by you and someone else in 1994; correct?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These photos are from 1994. They do not represent just some persons. This is my father, my brother and myself. But these photos do not represent the beatings. This is something else.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Perhaps you could tell us what they represent, then.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Ackerman asked me a question concerning my voluntary departure from the town and my answer was that I had been expelled. I stated that I was expelled in this manner, that I didn't leave voluntarily. That night, at least 20 and perhaps as many as 50 persons were beaten in the same manner and expelled from the town. 90 per cent of us sustained fractures and we did not leave the town on our own voluntarily. We were brutally made to leave our home town.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So these -- do you have anything to state about the admission of these photographs in evidence, Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: At this point?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, I don't think they have anything to do with an answer to my rather simple question: And that is, is it your contention that were you expelled from Prnjavor. I think his answer to that is yes, he doesn't have to go beyond that. I accept that answer. Except I have more questions about it. I have no desire for these to be part of the evidence.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The Trial Chamber simply doesn't agree with you at all, Mr. Ackerman. Those photographs are being admitted in evidence and they will be marked, please, find a number for them, Madam Registrar. When they are neither Prosecution witnesses or Defence witnesses, we had some instances before, I think we established -- we had a particular reference number that -- it's quite some time since we have had documents of this nature. So Madam Chuqing, please, will you be kind enough to identify sequential reference for these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honour, if you will allow me, I have prepared the same bunch of photographs for the Court. These are old copies and have been damaged. With your permission I would like to give you another set of the same photographs.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. Let's see the copies that you have available for the Court.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, while we are waiting for that I would like to request Your Honours to initiate an investigation as to how it is that an official statement from the OTP contains a statement purportedly by this witness and signed by him saying, "I am providing copies of these photographs," and the witness says that that's not true, he never did that. I think that deserves to be investigated. Somebody is not being square with Your Honours about this. And as you said, when Ms. Bondic was testifying -

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Wait a minute, because here we have more photos. This was not amongst the others.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Here they are.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Or at least I didn't see it. The rest seem okay. See if there is -- see if there is one like this. Oh, yes, okay. All right. Okay.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Could you count them, please, usher?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Your Honour, now we have other photos and some of them are roughly the same thing.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Sixteen. I have 16 here. How many do you have, usher?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Fifteen.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So someone must do the tallying. I think I saw one there which I don't recall seeing over there but anyway. In the meantime we've taken note of your request to initiate -- 15 or 16?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE JANU
utterances.text: Seventeen.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Seventeen?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So let's have the others as well and Judge Taya will do the tallying.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: In connection with my request that you look into this, Your Honour, I just want to remind you of your statement during the testimony of another witness here, that if you found that somebody was not being truthful with the Trial Chamber, you would come down very hard upon that person and there is some indication here that something is amiss. Because the statement says one thing and the witness says another.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes, we've taken note of that and we will decide at a later stage what to do about it.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: In the meantime, what shall we do, Mr. Ackerman? Shall we stop here?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. Maybe within the next several house we can get the count right. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MS. RICHTEROVA
utterances.text: Your Honour, I was informed that Mr. Odobasic is set to go back on Thursday because one other team requested his presence, but he can be postponed, his departure can be postponed until Friday so there is no problem.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we will stop here today, for today. Mr. Odobasic, we will continue tomorrow. In the meantime, we are keeping the originals too for the time being. We will give them back to you tomorrow morning, tomorrow afternoon. You don't have to worry about that. We just want to make sure that we have exactly the same number, the same copies. Judge Taya has already discovered that there are duplicates, at least of one photo. This one is duplicated. Actually, it's not. It's a different photo but -- but it is not a duplicate of the other. It's a different one. It's a different one. Mr. Ackerman, there are these two photos which at first sight, in the previous bundle, we had one of these, which one I wouldn't be able to tell you unless I make a comparison. If you look carefully, the two are very similar, almost identical, but they are two different, separates photos.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I think one or the other is sufficient but not both.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Yes. That would still bring it to 16, and we need to find the other extra one.

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: I assume you will have someone gather me up as usual to come to chambers.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Rheinhold, please will you attend to Mr. Ackerman and escort him to room 177 because otherwise --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: All right. So we give these two back -- we give these two back to the witness, together with the originals that he had handed to us. The situation, Mr. Ackerman -- Mr. Ackerman?

utterances.speaker: MR. ACKERMAN
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: The position is as explained to you there are these two which are not exactly duplicates but almost and we are only retaining one because we don't need two, and then there is this document, this document, which is of the same person, one with the trousers on and the other one without the trousers, with the underpants, and we are only retaining this because this is what was in the original bundle. So that goes there. And this is returned to the witness, together with this, this and that. Usher? And Madam Registrar, did you find the reference number for these documents?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Before we used some MFR marked for identification number but those documents actually later on were admitted into either OTP exhibit or Defence exhibit. Now if you want to admit these into Court exhibit perhaps we can use a "C" in the front.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: So we'll use a C in the front to make it easy. Why C and not TC?

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Well, it's up to you Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE AGIUS
utterances.text: Because we are not the Court, we are -- so it's TC 1 to 15. All right? Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
